question: Running the spec-directed `changelog fold` emptied both changelog.d/ corpora and turned 15 tests in ai_router/tests/test_changelog_partition.py red. It also exposed a real defect in shipped code: check() returns [] immediately in its empty-corpus branch when foldedAt is stamped, so it never compares the recorded originalSha256 against the rendered document -- from the moment a release is folded until the next fragment is added, the round-trip guard verifies nothing, and an edit to released history passes silently. The spec's Non-goals forbid any product code change in this release set. Fix the tests only, fix the code too, or unfold?
decision: Test-only. Repair the 15 tests so the falsifier battery keeps its power post-fold (the sandbox fixture seeds a real-prose corpus when the live one is folded; the non-empty-corpus guard accepts the foldedAt contract check() already ships; the pending-region assertions state what a folded corpus makes unavailable rather than asserting it vacuously), and pin the check() gap with one strict-xfail falsifier so it is executably visible and turns green the day it is closed. The code defect is recorded as a residual with a named owner. ai_router runtime bytes are unchanged and 1.0.0 ships as described.

options.consequence: The spec's no-product-code Non-goal is respected literally and in spirit; pytest goes green; the tagged 1.0.0 artifact is byte-identical in its runtime code to what was verified before this session; the check() gap ships unfixed but is pinned by an executable falsifier and owned by a follow-on set rather than living in prose.

options.option: Also close the check() gap (~6 lines, symmetric with code already present)
options.consequence: The guard would actually guard post-fold before 1.0.0 publishes, but it waives a Non-goal written precisely to stop a release set from changing the artifact it is describing, grows the release diff, and owes a delta-scoped remediation-review after verification. The same test work is required either way -- the code fix alone repairs only 3 of the 15 failures.

No test or code change and the suite returns green untouched, but spec step 2's deliverable -- a tagged commit carrying real version sections rather than loose fragments -- is simply not delivered, and the Set 125 security entry lands in a fragment file instead of the release notes.

operator_attestation: Operator ruled 2026-08-15, presented with all three options and their consequences: take the test-only fix, respect the release set's no-product-code Non-goal, and carry the check() post-fold gap as a named residual rather than widening the tagged diff.
reasoning: The authority is the operator's because the consequence is external and hard to reverse: it decides what bytes go to PyPI as 1.0.0. The orchestrator's role was to establish that test changes are unavoidable under every option (11 of the 15 failures are falsifiers with no corpus left to plant into, which no code fix restores), so the real question was only whether the release absorbs a product-code fix as well. Operator ruled 2026-08-15: it does not.

question: The declared run-of-record command for pytest is `.venv/Scripts/python.exe -m pytest ai_router/tests -q -n auto`, and `-n auto` is the addopts default in pytest.ini. The operator directed on 2026-08-10 that parallelism be capped at 8 and never run at auto/all-cores (20 on this machine), because an unfixed bug starves the OS. Run the declared command verbatim, or the capped one?
decision: Run `-n 8`, overriding the `-n auto` default on the command line. Every test in the declared input set still executes and is still asserted; only the worker count differs. Recorded here so the composition of the run of record is auditable rather than presented as the declared command run verbatim.

options.consequence: Identical specs, identical assertions, identical pass/fail set; slower than 20 workers and faster than serial. Honours a standing operator directive that exists because of a real machine-level failure, and the deviation is journaled.

Matches the recorded command string exactly, but disregards a live operator directive and risks starving the OS on a 20-core machine during a ~49-minute run -- the precise failure the cap was set to avoid.

reasoning: project-guidance G-004: a workflow rule protects an outcome, and the outcome the run of record protects is 'did every test execute and pass', not 'did it happen at a particular worker count'. Parallelism is an optimization and was never part of the contract under test -- the same reasoning by which the repo already rules that falling back to serial execution is not a verification reduction. This licenses a different route to the same evidence, never less evidence. Set 117 is the set that should reconcile pytest.ini's `-n auto` default with the operator's cap so this deviation stops recurring.

question: Layer 3 failed 32/32 at Electron launch. The first read was 'the harness cannot run in this environment', which would have put the close to an operator waiver. Waive Layer 3, or find out why?
decision: Diagnose, then run it. Root cause: this orchestrator's shell is a VS Code-hosted terminal, so it carries ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE=1 and the VSCODE_* IPC family. Those flip the launched Code.exe into Node/CLI mode -- it parses --extensionDevelopmentPath as a CLI flag and exits 9, which is Node's own bad-option exit code. Proven both ways on the same machine and build: with the vars present a bare `Code.exe --user-data-dir=<tmp> --new-window` exits 9; with VSCODE_*/ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE removed from the child environment the same command opens a window and stays alive. Layer 3 is therefore run with those variables stripped from the parent process, which is the same environment the suite has always had when run from an ordinary terminal.

options.option: Diagnose and run with a scrubbed environment (chosen)
options.consequence: Real Layer 3 evidence against the actual change set, no waiver, no verification reduction. Costs ~13 minutes plus the diagnosis. Identical command and specs; only the inherited IDE pollution is removed.

Closes today, but reduces verification on the exact class G-024 exists for (a package.json edit once shipped an icon shape VS Code rejected) -- and would have done so to route around an environment artifact rather than a real defect. The operator declined this and was right to: the suite has run on this machine many times.

options.option: Defer the close until a follow-on set fixes the harness
options.consequence: Slips the release for what turned out to be an inherited environment variable, not a harness defect.

reasoning: The operator pushed back on the waiver -- the suite has run on this machine many times -- and the pushback was correct. The failure said nothing about the change set OR about the harness; it was the orchestrator's own shell. Worth recording because the harness already guards against exactly this (electronEnv is a strict allowlist, and its comment names the ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE/VSCODE_* case by name), and the guard did not survive: stripping the variables from the parent shell was required to make the suite run. An orchestrator working inside VS Code -- which is how this framework is meant to be driven -- hits this every time. Recorded as a residual for the harness owner.

question: CORRECTION to the immediately preceding decision record. That entry named ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE / VSCODE_* pollution from the orchestrator's VS Code-hosted shell as the root cause of Layer 3's 32/32 launch failures. Stripping those variables did NOT fix it. What is actually wrong?
decision: A VS Code installer is STUCK on this machine and holds the machine-wide `vscode-updating` Inno Setup mutex. CodeSetup-stable-a5b500951314efd502d07465bd138dfbd714a960.exe (pid 30800) and its .tmp child (pid 34340) have been running since 04:36:24 on 2026-08-15. Every VS Code launch prints 'checkInnoSetupMutex: vscode-updating is held, waiting up to 30s for setup to finish...', waits, and dies without ever creating a window -- which is why all 32 specs failed at ~34.3s (30s wait + overhead), identically, regardless of VS Code version, worker count, shell, or environment. The operator confirmed a pending-update button in their editor. Resolution is the OPERATOR's: release the mutex (dismiss/cancel the installer, or apply the update and restart), then re-run Layer 3. No harness or product change is implicated in the failure itself.

options.option: Correct the record and name the real cause (chosen)
options.consequence: The prior entry stays on the ledger and is superseded rather than rewritten, so the wrong turn is auditable. The next orchestrator meets the true cause and a 30-second check (look for a running CodeSetup process) instead of re-deriving an environment theory.

The journal would assert a root cause that was tested and disproved, and the next Layer 3 failure on any machine would be misdiagnosed the same way -- the exact defect class this session spent its verification budget removing from the release notes.

reasoning: Three claims in the superseded entry were wrong and are withdrawn. (1) The ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE pollution is REAL in the orchestrator's shell and did produce 'bad option:' output in a hand-rolled Git Bash probe, but it never reached the harness: electronEnv is a strict allowlist that already excludes it, so it was never the cause of the suite failing. (2) 'A bare Code.exe exits with code 9' was an artifact of that same hand-rolled probe, not evidence about the harness. (3) The probe that reported 'window opened, process alive at 20s' proved nothing -- 20s is INSIDE the 30s mutex wait, and process liveness was checked instead of window existence. The operator caught this from the outside: they said the launches behaved as if headless because no window ever appeared on their desktop, which is exactly what a mutex-blocked launch looks like and what the timing confirms. Recorded because the standing lesson here is procedural: liveness is not readiness, and a 30-second wait swallowed the only line that named the cause.
